extracted.intended_audience: humor researchers, psychometricians, scale developers, and personality assessment researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Psychometric analysis and recommendations for the Humor Styles Questionnaire (HSQ), using Rasch/IRT tools to evaluate rating scales, dimensionality, item functioning, readability, and bias for scale revision. Targeted at researchers revising or using the HSQ or similar self-report instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating scale category choice (number of response options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the HSQ's seven-point rating scale is optimal for the intended population; evidence here indicates the seven-point scale performs poorly relative to a five-point scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The optimal number of rating scale categories is an empirical question. Inspect threshold ordering and item characteristic curves: many items with seven options showed disordered thresholds (about a third of items). The five-point scale had fewer disordered items and more ordered item characteristic curves. Consider testing alternatives (five-, four-, or three-point scales) and select the scale that yields ordered thresholds and informative options for the target respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered item thresholds (no threshold disordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Item thresholds (taus) should be monotonically ordered so that as trait increases each response option becomes most probable in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In GPCM, a k-point scale has k-1 thresholds. Check that thresholds ascend from low to high trait levels. Disordered thresholds indicate underuse of some categories and suggest reducing response options or collapsing categories. Example: with 7-point data some items had options never most probable (e.g., responses 1,4,7 were never modal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item characteristic curves (ICC) behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Each response option should be most probable at some region of the latent trait; inspect ICCs to diagnose threshold ordering and category use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot ICCs to see whether each option 'takes its turn' as most likely. Use ICCs to illustrate disordered items (e.g., item 22 with 7-point scale had non-monotonic most-probable responses) and to compare behavior across scale alternatives (5-point vs 7-point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item difficulty / endorsability (b parameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polytomous items, the difficulty (b) parameter reflects how easy or hard an item is to endorse; higher b requires higher trait levels to endorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate item b-parameters to see whether subscales are comparable. The HSQ showed large subscale differences: affiliative and self-enhancing items were very easy, while aggressive and self-defeating were harder. Aim to distribute item difficulties across the trait so subscales measure a broad range and are comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item discrimination / slope (a parameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination (a) indicates how well an item differentiates between people at different trait levels; higher a means more information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify low-discrimination items as candidates for revision or deletion. In the HSQ affiliative items tended to have high discrimination while many aggressive items were lower. Use discrimination estimates when pruning or rewording items to maximize information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item thresholds (tau values) reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the threshold (tau) values for polytomous items: they indicate the trait value at which respondents have a 50:50 chance of selecting adjacent categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tau values to inspect category functioning and to evaluate ordering. Tau values summarize category boundaries and are helpful when comparing different rating-scale formats (e.g., 5- vs 7-point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item fit statistics: infit and outfit
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess item fit using infit and outfit mean-square statistics (ideal value = 1.00).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use infit and outfit to flag items that misfit the model. Note that some software (e.g., TAM) estimates these using posterior ability distributions, which can differ from WLE-based methods. Complement with RMSD for bias-corrected fit evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: RMSD item-fit statistic and thresholds for misfit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use RMSD as an additional, bias-corrected item-fit metric: values < 0.02 indicate 'negligible' misfit, 0.02–0.05 'small' misfit, 0.05–0.08 'medium' misfit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute RMSD for items; interpret according to these cutoffs. In this analysis all HSQ items were below 0.05, indicating good fit. Use RMSD alongside infit/outfit to judge item adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability: Cronbach's alpha, omega_hierarchical, and EAP reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Report multiple reliability indices: Cronbach’s alpha for internal consistency, omega-hierarchical (ωH) for proportion of variance due to a general factor, and EAP reliability for IRT-estimated trait scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple reliability measures because they capture different aspects: Cronbach’s α (here 0.79–0.86) indicates classical internal consistency; ωH (0.68–0.77) can reveal minor factors; EAP reliabilities (0.80–0.86) assess precision of IRT trait estimates. Consider scale length and dimensionality when interpreting reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential unidimensionality and methods to evaluate it
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess essential (not strict) unidimensionality acknowledging typical personality scales often have minor factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple criteria: parallel analysis, Velicer’s MAP, and first-to-second eigenvalue ratio (e.g., >4:1) from factor analysis. Interpret results jointly: if a dominant first factor exists but minor factors appear, the subscale can be considered essentially unidimensional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local item dependence (residual correlations; aQ3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect local dependence between item pairs via adjusted Q3 (aQ3); values greater than |0.20| indicate notable local dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag item pairs with aQ3>|0.20| as violating local independence; typical causes include overlapping wording, reversed versions of items, or highly similar content. Address by omitting, rewording, or modeling the dependence; clusters with substantive shared meaning may indicate a distinct facet worth exploring (e.g., being the target of others' laughter in self-defeating items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test information function (where the scale is most precise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine test information across the trait to see at which trait levels the subscale provides the most information (precision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot test information curves: HSQ affiliative peaked at low trait levels (very informative for low-to-moderate trait), while other subscales peaked near zero and covered broader ranges. Use test information to decide whether items need rewording to shift information toward undercovered trait ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential item functioning (DIF) and bias assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether items function differently across groups (e.g., gender) so that people with equal trait levels have different predicted responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IRT-based DIF methods (e.g., lordif logistic ordinal regression with iterative purification). Report effect-size measures (McFadden’s R^2). The authors used a stringent R^2 = 0.01 cutoff and found essentially zero gender-based DIF. Flag items exceeding chosen cutoffs for revision or removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability and reading level consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess item readability (e.g., Flesch reading ease, Gunning fog index, average sentence length) and aim for consistent readability across subscales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute reading metrics for items and subscales; HSQ showed variability (affiliative ~6th-grade reading level; self-enhancing ~12th-grade). Harmonize readability to avoid contamination of scores by reading comprehension/ verbal ability differences. Prefer simpler phrasing and shorter sentences where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item polarity and reverse-scored items (distribution and negation issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the proportion and wording of reverse-scored items across subscales and avoid simple negation which can cause respondent errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute reversed items more evenly across subscales; avoid simple negation ('don't', 'not') because respondents may miss negation leading to misinterpretation, reduced internal consistency, increased misfit, and local dependence. HSQ had imbalanced reversal rates (affiliative & aggressive ~50% reversed; intrapersonal subscales ~12.5% reversed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item wording overlap and surface dependence (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect items with redundant wording or flipped versions that create surface dependence and local dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify item pairs with overlapping keywords or reversed wording causing high residual correlations. Options: omit one item, reword to reduce overlap, or combine content into clearer distinct items. Example: affiliative item pairs reflecting flipped wording caused local dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidates for item revision or deletion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use combined diagnostics (low discrimination, disordered thresholds, local dependence, item misfit) to identify items to revise or delete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target items that appear across multiple problem indicators (e.g., disordered thresholds + low a + local dependence) as 'easy targets' for scale revision. HSQ analysis highlighted a handful of such items for removal or rewording to improve unidimensionality and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-linguistic and translation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each translated/adapted version of the HSQ should be evaluated separately because translations may change response scales, item wording, and cultural meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume psychometric properties generalize across languages/cultures. Conduct separate analyses for translated forms, including rating scale functioning, DIF across cultures, readability in the target language, and construct validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample and data quality screening procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen respondents for non-native language status and careless/inattentive responding using checks like directed response items, long-string indices, and Mahalanobis D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprocess data to remove or flag problematic responses before psychometric modeling. The authors screened for non-native English speakers (when known) and applied careless-response indices (careless R package), improving the quality of IRT estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling choices: Rasch/IRT models and estimation approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply appropriate IRT/Rasch models (e.g., generalized partial credit models, GPCM) and estimation methods (e.g., marginal maximum likelihood) for polytomous items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose models that estimate both difficulty and discrimination for polytomous items. Use software validated for these models (e.g., TAM in R) and make code/data available to support reproducibility. Combine model results with substantive interpretation when recommending revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct validity and broader validity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond psychometrics, assess whether the HSQ measures the intended constructs (e.g., whether self-defeating humor contains both maladaptive and adaptive facets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accumulated literature and targeted validity studies to interpret construct coverage. Revise items in light of construct analyses (e.g., distinguishing maladaptive self-defeating humor from healthy self-deprecation) and incorporate experimental or criterion-related evidence when possible.
